recitals_and_articles.text: 1. The Board shall ensure the consistent application of this Regulation. To that end, the Board shall, on its own initiative or, where relevant, at the request of the Commission, in particular: (a) monitor and ensure the correct application of this Regulation in the cases provided for in Articles 64 and 65 without prejudice to the tasks of national supervisory authorities; (b) advise the Commission on any issue related to the protection of personal data in the Union, including on any proposed amendment of this Regulation; (c) advise the Commission on the format and procedures for the exchange of information between controllers, processors and supervisory authorities for binding corporate rules; (d) issue guidelines, recommendations, and best practices on procedures for erasing links, copies or replications of personal data from publicly available communication services as referred to in Article 17(2); (e) examine, on its own initiative, on request of one of its members or on request of the Commission, any question covering the application of this Regulation and issue guidelines, recommendations and best practices in order to encourage consistent application of this Regulation; (f) issue guidelines, recommendations and best practices in accordance with point (e) of this paragraph for further specifying the criteria and conditions for decisions based on profiling pursuant to Article 22(2); (g) issue guidelines, recommendations and best practices in accordance with point (e) of this paragraph for establishing the personal data breaches and determining the undue delay referred to in Article 33(1) and (2) and for the particular circumstances in which a controller or a processor is required to notify the personal data breach; (h) issue guidelines, recommendations and best practices in accordance with point (e) of this paragraph as to the circumstances in which a personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of the natural persons referred to in Article 34(1). (i) issue guidelines, recommendations and best practices in accordance with point (e) of this paragraph for the purpose of further specifying the criteria and requirements for personal data transfers based on binding corporate rules adhered to by controllers and binding corporate rules adhered to by processors and on further necessary requirements to ensure the protection of personal data of the data subjects concerned referred to in Article 47; (j) issue guidelines, recommendations and best practices in accordance with point (e) of this paragraph for the purpose of further specifying the criteria and requirements for the personal data transfers on the basis of Article 49(1); (k) draw up guidelines for supervisory authorities concerning the application of measures referred to in Article 58(1), (2) and (3) and the setting of administrative fines pursuant to Article 83; (l) review the practical application of the guidelines, recommendations and best practices referred to in points (e) and (f); (m) issue guidelines, recommendations and best practices in accordance with point (e) of this paragraph for establishing common procedures for reporting by natural persons of infringements of this Regulation pursuant to Article 54(2); (n) encourage the drawing-up of codes of conduct and the establishment of data protection certification mechanisms and data protection seals and marks pursuant to Articles 40 and 42; (o) carry out the accreditation of certification bodies and its periodic review pursuant to Article 43 and maintain a public register of accredited bodies pursuant to Article 43(6) and of the accredited controllers or processors established in third countries pursuant to Article 42(7); (p) specify the requirements referred to in Article 43(3) with a view to the accreditation of certification bodies under Article 42; (q) provide the Commission with an opinion on the certification requirements referred to in Article 43(8); (r) provide the Commission with an opinion on the icons referred to in Article 12(7); (s) provide the Commission with an opinion for the assessment of the adequacy of the level of protection in a third country or international organisation, including for the assessment whether a third country, a territory or one or more specified sectors within that third country, or an international organisation no longer ensures an adequate level of protection. To that end, the Commission shall provide the Board with all necessary documentation, including correspondence with the government of the third country, with regard to that third country, territory or specified sector, or with the international organisation. (t) issue opinions on draft decisions of supervisory authorities pursuant to the consistency mechanism referred to in Article 64(1), on matters submitted pursuant to Article 64(2) and to issue binding decisions pursuant to Article 65, including in cases referred to in Article 66; (u) promote the cooperation and the effective bilateral and multilateral exchange of information and best practices between the supervisory authorities; (v) promote common training programmes and facilitate personnel exchanges between the supervisory authorities and, where appropriate, with the supervisory authorities of third countries or with international organisations; (w) promote the exchange of knowledge and documentation on data protection legislation and practice with data protection supervisory authorities worldwide. (x) issue opinions on codes of conduct drawn up at Union level pursuant to Article 40(9); and (y) maintain a publicly accessible electronic register of decisions taken by supervisory authorities and courts on issues handled in the consistency mechanism.

recitals_and_articles.text: 2. Administrative fines shall, depending on the circumstances of each individual case, be imposed in addition to, or instead of, measures referred to in points (a) to (h) and (j) of Article 58(2). recitals_and_articles.text: 1. Processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes, shall be subject to appropriate safeguards, in accordance with this Regulation, for the rights and freedoms of the data subject. Those safeguards shall ensure that technical and organisational measures are in place in particular in order to ensure respect for the principle of data minimisation. Those measures may include pseudonymisation provided that those purposes can be fulfilled in that manner. Where those purposes can be fulfilled by further processing which does not permit or no longer permits the identification of data subjects, those purposes shall be fulfilled in that manner.

akn4eu_ancestry: Article 98 — Review of other Union legal acts on data protection
recitals_and_articles.text: The Commission shall, if appropriate, submit legislative proposals with a view to amending other Union legal acts on the protection of personal data, in order to ensure uniform and consistent protection of natural persons with regard to processing. canonical_edges.reasoning: Operative item 1 directly construes Article 2(1) and (2) GDPR to apply to commercial third-country transfers irrespective of subsequent public-authority processing for national-security purposes.

canonical_edges.reasoning: Operative item 5 is a direct validity ruling. The Privacy Shield was adopted under Article 45(3) GDPR but its substantive purpose was to provide a transfer pathway; the court invalidates it because the Commission's finding that the US ensures an adequate level of protection disregarded the requirements of Article 45(3) GDPR read with Articles 7, 8 and 47 of the Charter. Article 45(3) does not have a dedicated 'interprets' edge here because the court did not construe Article 45(3) beyond holding the implementing act invalid; the validity outcome 'invalid' is recorded on this edge. Article 46(1) is the narrowest existing single-paragraph target that the invalidity finding is grounded in (in conjunction with the Charter and the Article 45(3) procedural standard).

verification_quotes.quote: Therefore, the ombudsperson mechanism to which the Privacy Shield Decision refers does not provide any cause of action before a body which offers the persons whose data is transferred to the United States guarantees essentially equivalent to those required by Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights.

Therefore, in finding, in Article 1(1) of the Privacy Shield Decision, that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred from the Union to organisations in that third country under the EU-US Privacy Shield, the Commission disregarded the requirements of Article 45(3) of the GDPR, read in the light of Articles 7, 8 and 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights.

verification_quotes.quote: Although Article 46 of the GDPR does not specify the nature of the requirements which flow from that reference to 'appropriate safeguards', 'enforceable rights' and 'effective legal remedies', it should nevertheless be interpreted in the light of the overall scheme and purpose of that regulation in order to ensure a high level of protection of natural persons in the context of the processing of personal data.

Therefore, the answer to the second, third and sixth questions is that Article 46(1) and Article 46(2)(c) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the appropriate safeguards, enforceable rights and effective legal remedies required by those provisions must ensure that data subjects whose personal data are transferred to a third country pursuant to standard data protection clauses are afforded a level of protection essentially equivalent to that guaranteed within the European Union by that regulation, read in the light of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union.

verification_quotes.quote: Accordingly, the information provided to the data subject pursuant to the right of access provided for in Article 15(1)(c) of the GDPR must be as precise as possible. In particular, that right of access entails the ability of the data subject to obtain from the controller information about the specific recipients to whom the data have been or will be disclosed or, alternatively, to elect merely to request information concerning the categories of recipient.

Accordingly, it may be accepted that, in specific circumstances, it is not possible to provide information about specific recipients. Therefore, the right of access may be restricted to information about categories of recipient if it is impossible to disclose the identity of specific recipients, in particular where they are not yet known.

In addition, it should be borne in mind that, under Article 12(5)(b) of the GDPR, the controller may, pursuant to the principle of responsibility referred to in Article 5(2) and recital 74 of that regulation, refuse to act on requests from a data subject where those requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive, it being specified that it is for the controller to demonstrate that those requests are unfounded or excessive.

In the light of all the foregoing considerations, the answer to the question referred for a preliminary ruling is that Article 15(1)(c) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the data subject’s right of access to personal data concerning him or her, provided for by that provision, entails, where those data have been or will be disclosed to recipients, an obligation on the part of the controller to provide the data subject with the actual identity of those recipients, unless it is impossible to identify those recipients or the controller demonstrates that the data subject’s requests for access are manifestly unfounded or excessive within the meaning of Article 12(5) of the GDPR, in which cases the controller may indicate to the data subject only the categories of recipient in question.

case_law_relations.holding: Article 15(1)(c) GDPR entitles the data subject to the actual identities of recipients to whom data have been or will be disclosed; the controller may give categories only if identifying specific recipients is impossible or if the controller demonstrates that the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive under Article 12(5) GDPR.

verification_quotes.quote: Accordingly, the information provided to the data subject pursuant to the right of access provided for in Article 15(1)(c) of the GDPR must be as precise as possible. In particular, that right of access entails the ability of the data subject to obtain from the controller information about the specific recipients to whom the data have been or will be disclosed or, alternatively, to elect merely to request information concerning the categories of recipient.

Accordingly, it may be accepted that, in specific circumstances, it is not possible to provide information about specific recipients. Therefore, the right of access may be restricted to information about categories of recipient if it is impossible to disclose the identity of specific recipients, in particular where they are not yet known.

In addition, it should be borne in mind that, under Article 12(5)(b) of the GDPR, the controller may, pursuant to the principle of responsibility referred to in Article 5(2) and recital 74 of that regulation, refuse to act on requests from a data subject where those requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive, it being specified that it is for the controller to demonstrate that those requests are unfounded or excessive.

In the light of all the foregoing considerations, the answer to the question referred for a preliminary ruling is that Article 15(1)(c) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the data subject’s right of access to personal data concerning him or her, provided for by that provision, entails, where those data have been or will be disclosed to recipients, an obligation on the part of the controller to provide the data subject with the actual identity of those recipients, unless it is impossible to identify those recipients or the controller demonstrates that the data subject’s requests for access are manifestly unfounded or excessive within the meaning of Article 12(5) of the GDPR, in which cases the controller may indicate to the data subject only the categories of recipient in question.

case_law_relations.holding: Article 6(1) GDPR — points (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and (f) are construed for the social-network context: (b) requires objective indispensability for a purpose integral to the contract; (f) requires informed notice, strict necessity, and balancing; (c) requires an objective of public interest, proportionality and strict necessity; (d) and (e) in principle do not justify the cross-service processing; (a) is not precluded by dominant position alone but dominant position is an important factor.

verification_quotes.quote: In the light of all the foregoing, the answer to Questions 3 and 4 is that point (b) of the first subparagraph of Article 6(1) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the processing of personal data by the operator of an online social network … can be regarded as necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subjects are party, within the meaning of that provision, only on condition that the processing is objectively indispensable for a purpose that is integral to the contractual obligation intended for those users, such that the main subject matter of the contract cannot be achieved if that processing does not occur.

Point (f) of the first subparagraph of Article 6(1) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that such processing can be regarded as necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party, within the meaning of that provision, only on condition that the operator has informed the users from whom the data have been collected of a legitimate interest that is pursued by the data processing, that such processing is carried out only in so far as is strictly necessary for the purposes of that legitimate interest and that it is apparent from a balancing of the opposing interests, having regard to all the relevant circumstances, that the interests or fundamental freedoms and rights of those users do not override that legitimate interest of the controller or of a third party.

In the light of the foregoing, the answer to Question 5 is that point (c) of the first subparagraph of Article 6(1) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the processing of personal data by the operator of an online social network … is justified, under that provision, where it is actually necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject, pursuant to a provision of EU law or the law of the Member State concerned, where that legal basis meets an objective of public interest and is proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued and where that processing is carried out only in so far as is strictly necessary.

Points (d) and (e) of the first subparagraph of Article 6(1) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that such processing of personal data cannot, in principle and subject to verification by the referring court, be regarded as necessary in order to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person, within the meaning of point (d), or for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller, within the meaning of point (e).

In the light of the foregoing, the answer to Question 6 is that point (a) of the first subparagraph of Article 6(1) and Article 9(2)(a) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the fact that the operator of an online social network holds a dominant position on the market for online social networks does not, as such, preclude the users of such a network from being able validly to consent, within the meaning of Article 4(11) of that regulation, to the processing of their personal data by that operator. This is nevertheless an important factor in determining whether the consent was in fact validly and, in particular, freely given, which it is for that operator to prove.

case_law_relations.reasoning: Operative item 2 directly construes Article 9(1).
case_law_relations.holding: Article 9(1) GDPR must be interpreted as covering collection of special-category data via integrated interfaces, cookies or similar technologies from third-party sites/apps, with linking to the user's social-network account, where the data processing reveals information falling within the special categories.

verification_quotes.quote: In the light of the foregoing, the answer to Question 2(a) is that Article 9(1) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that, where the user of an online social network visits websites or apps to which one or more of the categories referred to in that provision relate and, as the case may be, enters information into them when registering or when placing online orders, the processing of personal data by the operator of that online social network, which entails the collection – by means of integrated interfaces, cookies or similar storage technologies – of data from visits to those sites and apps and of the information entered by the user, the linking of all those data with the user's social network account and the use of those data by that operator, must be regarded as 'processing of special categories of personal data' within the meaning of that provision, which is in principle prohibited, subject to the derogations provided for in Article 9(2), where that data processing allows information falling within one of those categories to be revealed, irrespective of whether that information concerns a user of that network or any other natural person.

case_law_relations.reasoning: Operative item 3 directly construes Article 9(2)(e); Article 9(2) is the narrowest existing paragraph containing the derogations list.
case_law_relations.holding: Article 9(2)(e) GDPR — visiting such sites/apps does not constitute manifestly making public; explicit prior individual choice is required.

verification_quotes.quote: In the light of the foregoing, the answer to Question 2(b) is that Article 9(2)(e) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that, where the user of an online social network visits websites or apps to which the categories set out in Article 9(1) of the GDPR relate, the user does not manifestly make public, within the meaning of the first of those provisions, the data relating to those visits collected by the operator of that online social network via cookies or similar storage technologies; where he or she enters information into such websites or apps or where he or she clicks or taps on buttons integrated into those sites and apps, such as the 'Like' or 'Share' buttons or buttons enabling the user to identify himself or herself on those sites or apps using login credentials linked to his or her social network user account, his or her telephone number or email address, that user manifestly makes public, within the meaning of Article 9(2)(e), the data thus entered or resulting from the clicking or tapping on those buttons only in the circumstance where he or she has explicitly made the choice beforehand, as the case may be on the basis of individual settings selected with full knowledge of the facts, to make the data relating to him or her publicly accessible to an unlimited number of persons.

case_law_relations.reasoning: Paragraphs 39-43 of the operative reasons interpret Article 4(7) GDPR: the definition of 'controller' is broad and includes legal persons, and the EU legislature did not distinguish between natural and legal persons for the purposes of liability under the GDPR, subject solely to the condition that the person (alone or jointly) determines the purposes and means of processing. This is recorded as an interpretation of Article 4 (subunit (7)) within the existing article-Art4-Para1 block (the definition article has only one canonical paragraph node in the GDPR base graph; sub-unit (7) is captured in akn4eu_sub_units).
case_law_relations.holding: Article 4(7) of the GDPR defines the concept of 'controller' broadly, as referring to the natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data. The EU legislature did not distinguish, for the purposes of determining liability under that regulation, between natural persons and legal persons, that liability being subject to the sole condition that those persons, alone or jointly with others, determine the purposes and means of processing of personal data.

verification_quotes.quote: Article 4(7) of the GDPR defines the concept of 'controller' broadly, as referring to the natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data.

It therefore follows from the wording and purpose of Article 4(7) of the GDPR that the EU legislature did not distinguish, for the purposes of determining liability under that regulation, between natural persons and legal persons, that liability being subject to the sole condition that those persons, alone or jointly with others, determine the purposes and means of processing of personal data.

case_law_relations.reasoning: Paragraphs 45-47, 51, 71 and operative ruling 1 interpret Article 58(2) GDPR (specifically Article 58(2)(i)). The Court holds that Article 58(2) sets out the supervisory authorities' corrective powers in detail, without referring to Member-State law or leaving discretion, and that the power under Article 58(2)(i) to impose an administrative fine may be exercised directly against a legal person acting as controller, without prior identification of a natural person. The Member State may regulate the procedure but may not impose substantive conditions beyond Article 83(1) to (6).
case_law_relations.holding: It follows from a combined reading of Article 4(7), Article 83 and Article 58(2)(i) of the GDPR that an administrative fine in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) may also be imposed on legal persons where they are controllers. No provision of the GDPR permits the inference that the imposition of an administrative fine on a legal person as a controller is subject to a previous finding that that infringement was committed by an identified natural person.

verification_quotes.quote: Next, it must be stated that Article 58(2) of the GDPR sets out in detail the supervisory authorities' corrective powers, without referring to the law of the Member States or leaving any discretion to those States. First, those powers, which include, under Article 58(2)(i) of the GDPR, the power to impose an administrative fine, relate to the controller and, second, such a controller may, as is apparent from paragraph 39 of the present judgment, be a natural person or a legal person.

Article 58(2)(i) and Article 83(1) to (6) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 ... must be interpreted as precluding national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person.

case_law_relations.reasoning: Paragraphs 60, 65, 75, 78 and operative rulings 1 and 2 interpret Article 83(1) to (6) of the GDPR collectively, including Article 83(4) as the first of the three graduated infringement tiers. The Court holds that the substantive conditions for fines in Article 83(4) to (6) are exhaustively governed by EU law and that fines under any of those tiers are precluded from being conditioned on prior attribution to an identified natural person. Article 83(4) is one of the specific tiers whose substantive conditions the Court construes; accordingly, the judgment is mapped to article-Art83-Para4 as part of the operative ruling that Article 83(1) to (6) precludes national attribution-to-natural-person requirements.
case_law_relations.holding: Article 83(4) to (6) of the GDPR must be interpreted as precluding national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person; and as meaning that an administrative fine may be imposed pursuant to Article 83 only where it is established that the controller, which is both a legal person and an undertaking, intentionally or negligently committed an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) thereof.

verification_quotes.quote: In the light of the foregoing, the answer to the first question must be that Article 58(2)(i) and Article 83(1) to (6) of the GDPR must be interpreted as precluding national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person.

Having regard to the foregoing, the answer to the second question is that Article 83 of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that an administrative fine may be imposed pursuant to that provision only where it is established that the controller, which is both a legal person and an undertaking, intentionally or negligently committed an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) thereof.

case_law_relations.reasoning: The same operative holdings (paragraphs 60, 65, 75, 78; operative rulings 1 and 2) interpret Article 83(1) to (6) collectively, including Article 83(5) as the second graduated infringement tier. The ruling that substantive conditions for fines (fault requirement, no Member-State substantive additions) are exhaustively governed by EU law applies equally to Article 83(5).
case_law_relations.holding: Article 83(5) is part of the range exhaustively regulated by Article 83(1) to (6) GDPR; the same interpretation (no prior attribution to natural person; intentional or negligent infringement required) applies to fines imposed under that tier.

verification_quotes.quote: the substantive conditions which a supervisory authority must satisfy when it imposes an administrative fine on a controller are governed solely by EU law, since those conditions are laid down, in detail and without leaving any discretion to the Member States, in Article 83(1) to (6) of the GDPR

Article 83 of the GDPR does not allow an administrative fine to be imposed in respect of an infringement referred to in paragraphs 4 to 6 thereof, without it being established that that infringement was committed intentionally or negligently by the controller and that, consequently, a culpable infringement constitutes a condition for such a fine to be imposed.

case_law_relations.reasoning: Paragraphs 60, 65, 75, 78 and operative rulings 1 and 2 interpret Article 83(1) to (6) collectively, including Article 83(6) (non-compliance with an order by the supervisory authority referred to in Article 58(2)). The same exhaustive-EU-law and fault-requirement holdings apply to fines under Article 83(6). In the present case, the underlying infringement under Article 83(4) to (6) was specifically identified in the referring court's question and the operative ruling expressly references 'Article 83(4) to (6)' as the infringement class the controller may be fined for; Article 83(6) is part of that range.
case_law_relations.holding: Article 83(6) is part of the range exhaustively regulated by Article 83(1) to (6) GDPR; fines under Article 83(6) for non-compliance with an Article 58(2) order against a legal-person controller are likewise subject to the same substantive conditions (no prior attribution to a natural person; intentional or negligent infringement required).

verification_quotes.quote: Article 83 of the GDPR does not allow an administrative fine to be imposed in respect of an infringement referred to in paragraphs 4 to 6 thereof, without it being established that that infringement was committed intentionally or negligently by the controller and that, consequently, a culpable infringement constitutes a condition for such a fine to be imposed.

Article 58(2)(i) and Article 83(1) to (6) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 ... must be interpreted as precluding national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person.

case_law_relations.reasoning: The Court holds (paragraph 56, restated in paragraph 63) that the data subject enjoys the right under Article 15(1)(h) GDPR to obtain from the controller that establishes the probability value 'meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing'; without this, the right of access would be hollowed out, as the third-party recipient does not have that information. This is a binding interpretation of Article 15(1)(h), which is part of Article 15(1).
case_law_relations.holding: Article 15(1)(h) GDPR requires the controller that establishes the creditworthiness probability value to disclose meaningful information about the logic involved, the significance and the envisaged consequences of the automated decision-making, lest the data subject's right of access become ineffective in a multi-stakeholder scoring scenario.
case_law_relations.procedural_posture: Preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU from the Verwaltungsgericht Wiesbaden (Administrative Court, Wiesbaden, Germany); reference decision of 1 October 2021, received at the Court on 15 October 2021

verification_quotes.quote: the data subject enjoys, under Article 15(1)(h) of that regulation, the right to obtain from the controller, in particular, 'meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject'.

case_law_relations.reasoning: The Court expressly interprets Article 22(1) GDPR as covering the automated establishment of a probability value (scoring) by a credit information agency where a third party draws strongly on that value. This is the principal holding of the judgment and constrains the meaning of the 'decision' element in Article 22(1).
case_law_relations.holding: Article 22(1) GDPR covers the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value concerning a person's ability to meet payment commitments in the future, where a third party draws strongly on that value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.
case_law_relations.procedural_posture: Preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU from the Verwaltungsgericht Wiesbaden (Administrative Court, Wiesbaden, Germany); reference decision of 1 October 2021, received at the Court on 15 October 2021

verification_quotes.quote: Article 22(1) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value based on personal data relating to a person and concerning his or her ability to meet payment commitments in the future constitutes 'automated individual decision-making' within the meaning of that provision, where a third party, to which that probability value is transmitted, draws strongly on that probability value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.

case_law_relations.reasoning: The holding directs national courts to assess whether Member-State law (e.g. Paragraph 31 BDSG) can serve as a legal basis under Article 22(2)(b) GDPR for automated scoring; the judgment sets out the conditions of lawful authorisation under Article 22(2)(b) and explains how Article 22(2) interacts with Articles 5 and 6 GDPR (paragraphs 65-69).
case_law_relations.holding: Article 22(2)(b) GDPR requires the Member-State law authorising automated individual decision-making to lay down suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and legitimate interests; that law must comply with Articles 5 and 6 GDPR, and Member States are not empowered to add substantive lawfulness rules beyond Article 6(1)(c) and (e).
case_law_relations.procedural_posture: Preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU from the Verwaltungsgericht Wiesbaden (Administrative Court, Wiesbaden, Germany); reference decision of 1 October 2021, received at the Court on 15 October 2021

verification_quotes.quote: Thus, in the event that the law of a Member State authorises, under Article 22(2)(b) of the GDPR, the adoption of a decision solely based on automated processing, that processing must comply not only with the conditions set out in the latter provision and in Article 22(4) of that regulation, but also with the requirements set out in Articles 5 and 6 of that regulation.

case_law_relations.reasoning: The Court explicitly affirms (paragraph 66) that the suitable measures required under Article 22(2)(b) and, a fortiori, the safeguards under Article 22(3) include 'at least the right for the data subject to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express his or her point of view and to challenge the decision'; this is a direct interpretation of the safeguards enumerated in Article 22(3).
case_law_relations.holding: Article 22(3) GDPR safeguards (human intervention, expression of point of view, contestation) are integral to any automated decision-making falling within Article 22(1), including scoring by a credit information agency.
case_law_relations.procedural_posture: Preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU from the Verwaltungsgericht Wiesbaden (Administrative Court, Wiesbaden, Germany); reference decision of 1 October 2021, received at the Court on 15 October 2021

verification_quotes.quote: Those measures include, moreover, at least the right for the data subject to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express his or her point of view and to challenge the decision taken in his or her regard.

case_law_relations.reasoning: C-340/21 paragraphs 48–57 apply Article 24(1) GDPR (read with Article 5(2) and Article 32(1)) to allocate the burden of proof in an Article 82 action: the controller, not the data subject, bears the burden of proving the appropriateness of the security measures. The 'applies' predicate is appropriate here because the Court applies Article 24 to the procedural question of burden of proof rather than construing its substantive meaning.
pinpoints: C-340/21 paragraph 51 (Article 24(1) read with recital 74 — controller must implement appropriate measures and be able to demonstrate compliance)
C-340/21 paragraph 52 (wording of Article 5(2), Article 24(1) and Article 32(1) places burden on controller)
C-340/21 paragraph 57 (operative answer to first part of Question 3)
case_law_relations.holding: Article 24(1) GDPR, read in conjunction with Article 5(2) and Article 32(1), must be interpreted as meaning that in an Article 82 action the controller bears the burden of proving that the security measures implemented by it are appropriate under Article 32.
case_law_relations.procedural_posture: preliminary ruling — applications and interpretation of burden of proof

verification_quotes.pinpoint: C-340/21 paragraph 57 (operative answer to first part of Question 3)
verification_quotes.quote: The principle of accountability of the controller, set out in Article 5(2) of Regulation 2016/679 and given expression in Article 24 thereof, must be interpreted as meaning that, in an action for damages under Article 82 of that regulation, the controller in question bears the burden of proving that the security measures implemented by it are appropriate pursuant to Article 32 of that regulation.

case_law_relations.reasoning: C-340/21 paragraphs 40–47 interpret Article 32(1) GDPR: the appropriateness of technical and organisational measures must be assessed in two stages (identification of risks; verification of appropriate measures), and the controller has discretion but the national court must be able to evaluate the substance of the measures against the criteria in Article 32(1) (state of the art, costs, nature, scope, context, purposes).
pinpoints: C-340/21 paragraph 41 (recap of Article 32 assessment criteria)
C-340/21 paragraph 42 (two-stage concrete assessment; identifies the risks and possible consequences, then measures' appropriateness)
C-340/21 paragraph 43 (controller's discretion is not a bar to judicial review)
case_law_relations.holding: Article 32(1) GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the appropriateness of the technical and organisational measures implemented by the controller must be assessed by the national courts in a concrete manner, taking into account the risks associated with the processing and assessing whether the nature, content and implementation of those measures are appropriate to those risks.

verification_quotes.quote: Article 32 of Regulation 2016/679 must be interpreted as meaning that the appropriateness of the technical and organisational measures implemented by the controller under that article must be assessed by the national courts in a concrete manner, by taking into account the risks associated with the processing concerned and by assessing whether the nature, content and implementation of those measures are appropriate to those risks.

It is apparent from Article 32(1) and (2) that the appropriateness of such organisational and technical measures must be assessed in two stages. First, it is necessary to identify the risks of a personal data breach caused by the processing concerned and their possible consequences for the rights and freedoms of natural persons. … Secondly, it is necessary to ascertain whether the measures implemented by the controller are appropriate to those risks, taking into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation and the nature, scope, context and purposes of that processing.

case_law_relations.reasoning: C-340/21 paragraph 41 expressly reads Article 32(2) GDPR as the non-exhaustive list of factors to take into account when assessing the appropriate level of security (in particular the risks of accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data); paragraphs 45–46 apply that framework to the concrete analysis of the controller's measures.
pinpoints: C-340/21 paragraph 41 (Article 32(2) lists in a non-exhaustive manner the factors relevant for assessing the appropriate level of security)
C-340/21 paragraphs 45–46 (concrete-application factors tying back to Article 32(2))
case_law_relations.holding: Article 32(2) GDPR must be interpreted as setting the non-exhaustive assessment criteria — especially the risks of accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data — that the national court must apply when reviewing the appropriateness of the technical and organisational measures under Article 32(1).

verification_quotes.quote: In addition, paragraph 2 of that article lists, in a non-exhaustive manner, a number of factors that are relevant for assessing the level of safety appropriate to the risks posed by the processing concerned.

case_law_relations.reasoning: C-340/21 paragraph 50 reads Article 5(1)(f) GDPR (the integrity and confidentiality principle) as requiring the controller to ensure appropriate security of personal data via appropriate technical or organisational measures and to be able to demonstrate compliance. The integrity/confidentiality principle is the substantive standard to which Article 32 measures must give effect in an Article 82 action.
pinpoints: C-340/21 paragraph 50 (Article 5(1)(f) integrity and confidentiality principle)
C-340/21 paragraph 51 (Article 24(1) and Article 32(1) implement that principle)
C-340/21 paragraph 52 (reading of Article 5(2), Article 24(1) and Article 32(1) — all three must be applied in Article 82 actions)
case_law_relations.holding: Article 5(1)(f) GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the integrity and confidentiality obligation requires the controller to process personal data in a manner that ensures appropriate security via appropriate technical and organisational measures, and to be able to demonstrate compliance with that principle.

verification_quotes.quote: In particular, the controller must, in accordance with the principle of integrity and confidentiality of personal data laid down in Article 5(1)(f) of that regulation, make sure that such data are processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of those data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures, and must be able to demonstrate compliance with that principle.

case_law_relations.reasoning: C-340/21 paragraph 49 reads Article 5(2) GDPR as the textual basis of the accountability principle and paragraph 52 derives from Article 5(2) (together with Article 24(1) and Article 32(1)) that the controller bears the burden of demonstrating the appropriateness of security measures in Article 82 proceedings. Operative point 3 speaks of Article 5(2) as the principle that gives expression to Article 24.
pinpoints: C-340/21 paragraph 49 (Article 5(2) establishes the accountability principle)
C-340/21 paragraph 52 (wording of Article 5(2), Article 24(1) and Article 32(1) places burden on controller)
C-340/21 paragraph 57 (operative answer referencing 'the principle of accountability of the controller, set out in Article 5(2) of Regulation 2016/679')
case_law_relations.holding: Article 5(2) GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the accountability principle it establishes places the burden on the controller to demonstrate compliance with the principles in Article 5(1), including the integrity and confidentiality obligation in Article 5(1)(f), and the appropriateness of the Article 32 security measures in Article 82 proceedings.

verification_quotes.quote: It should be recalled that Article 5(2) of the GDPR establishes a principle of accountability, under which the controller is responsible for compliance with the principles relating to the processing of personal data set out in paragraph 1 of that article, and provides that that controller must be able to demonstrate compliance with those principles.

case_law_relations.reasoning: C-340/21 paragraphs 77–82 build on and directly apply C-300/21, re-affirming (i) the three cumulative conditions, (ii) the broad interpretation of damage and the rejection of a seriousness threshold, and (iii) the inclusion of mere loss of control as a non-material damage. The Court explicitly extends this to fear of future misuse as capable, in itself, of constituting non-material damage (paragraphs 80–86, operative point 6).
pinpoints: C-340/21 paragraph 77 (re-affirms three cumulative conditions citing C-300/21 paragraph 32)
C-340/21 paragraph 78 (re-affirms no-threshold rule citing C-300/21 paragraph 51)
C-340/21 paragraphs 80–82 (wording and recital 146 support broad interpretation, including 'loss of control')
C-340/21 paragraphs 85–86 (fear of future misuse capable of constituting non-material damage)
case_law_relations.holding: Article 82(1) GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the fear experienced by a data subject with regard to a possible misuse of his or her personal data by third parties as a result of an infringement of the GDPR is capable, in itself, of constituting 'non-material damage'.

verification_quotes.quote: Article 82(1) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the fear experienced by a data subject with regard to a possible misuse of his or her personal data by third parties as a result of an infringement of that regulation is capable, in itself, of constituting 'non-material damage' within the meaning of that provision.

It is apparent from that illustrative list of types of 'damage' that may be suffered by the data subjects that the EU legislature intended to include in those concepts, in particular, the mere 'loss of control' over their own data, as a result of an infringement of that regulation, even if there had been no misuse of the data in question to the detriment of those data subjects.

case_law_relations.reasoning: C-340/21 paragraphs 65–74 interpret Article 82(2) and (3) together: Article 82(2) GDPR establishes that the controller is liable for damage caused by processing that infringes the GDPR; the controller can escape only by proving it is in no way responsible for the event giving rise to the damage (Article 82(3)). The first two sentences of recital 146 GDPR (cited at paragraph 68) are the textual bridge between paragraphs 2 and 3.
pinpoints: C-340/21 paragraph 68 (first and second sentences of recital 146)
C-340/21 paragraph 69 (controller must, in principle, make good any damage)
C-340/21 paragraph 70 (strictly limited exemption — 'in any way')
C-340/21 paragraphs 71–72 (third-party cyberattack does not automatically exempt the controller)
case_law_relations.holding: Article 82(2) GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the controller is liable for damage caused by an infringement of the GDPR linked to its processing, and is exempt under Article 82(3) only on condition of proving that it is in no way responsible for the event giving rise to the damage.

verification_quotes.quote: Article 82(3) of Regulation 2016/679 must be interpreted as meaning that the controller cannot be exempt from its obligation to pay compensation for the damage suffered by a data subject, under Article 82(1) and (2) of that regulation, solely because that damage is a result of unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data by a 'third party', within the meaning of Article 4(10) of that regulation, in which case that controller must then prove that it is in no way responsible for the event that gave rise to the damage concerned.

case_law_relations.reasoning: C-340/21 is the operative judicial interpretation of Article 82(3) GDPR: the exemption must be strictly limited to cases where the controller proves it is in no way responsible for the event giving rise to the damage (paragraphs 65–74, operative point 5). The 'in any way' qualifier is expressly highlighted as the legislative intent to narrow the exemption.
pinpoints: C-340/21 paragraph 70 (words 'in any way' added during the legislative process; exemption must be strictly limited)
C-340/21 paragraphs 71–72 (third-party cyberattack does not automatically exempt the controller)
case_law_relations.holding: Article 82(3) GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the controller cannot be exempt from its obligation to pay compensation under Article 82(1) and (2) solely because the damage is the result of unauthorised access by a third party; the controller must then prove that it is in no way responsible for the event giving rise to the damage.

verification_quotes.quote: Thus, as is apparent from the express addition of the words 'in any way' during the legislative process, the circumstances in which the controller may claim to be exempt from civil liability under Article 82 of the GDPR must be strictly limited to those in which the controller is able to demonstrate that the damage is not attributable to it.

Article 82(3) of Regulation 2016/679 must be interpreted as meaning that the controller cannot be exempt from its obligation to pay compensation for the damage suffered by a data subject, under Article 82(1) and (2) of that regulation, solely because that damage is a result of unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data by a 'third party' …

case_law.procedural_posture: Revision; Aufhebung OLG Köln 7.12.2023 teilweise; im Übrigen Zurückweisung der Revision. Vorinstanz LG (250 € Schadensersatz zugesprochen); Berufung OLG Köln wies vollständig ab.
case_law.interpretation_issue: Höhe des immateriellen Schadensersatzes nach Art. 82 Abs. 1 DSGVO bei kurzzeitigem Kontrollverlust über eigene personenbezogene Daten (Facebook-Scraping-Vorfall).
case_law.holding: Bei einem bloßen Kontrollverlust über personenbezogene Daten ohne darüber hinausgehende psychische Beeinträchtigung hält der Senat eine Entschädigung in einer Größenordnung von 100 € als mit dem Effektivitätsgrundsatz vereinbar; eine Festsetzung in 'gegebenenfalls nur einstelliger Höhe' ist äußerst zweifelhaft. Schadensersatz nach Art. 82 Abs. 1 DSGVO darf weder hinter dem vollständigen Ausgleich zurückbleiben noch über ihn hinausgehen.
reasoning: Tatrichter hat bei Schätzung nach § 287 ZPO die Sensibilität der Daten (Art. 9 Abs. 1 DSGVO), Art des Kontrollverlusts (begrenzter/unbegrenzter Empfängerkreis), Dauer und Möglichkeit der Wiedererlangung der Kontrolle zu berücksichtigen (Rn. 99).

Senat schließt sich ausdrücklich der EuGH-Linie an, dass der immaterielle Schaden nicht weniger schwer wiegt als bei einer Körperverletzung (Rn. 97, unter Verweis auf EuGH C-200/23 Rn. 151 und C-182/22 Rn. 39 – Scalable Capital).
Bei bloßem Kontrollverlust indiziert der Senat 100 € als effektiven Ausgleich und lehnt OLG Celle (5 U 31/23 Rn. 102) als obiter abweichende Bemessung ab (Rn. 100).

pinpoints.quote_verbatim: Ist nach den Feststellungen des Gerichts allein ein Schaden in Form eines Kontrollverlusts an personenbezogenen Daten gegeben, weil weitere Schäden nicht nachgewiesen sind, hat der Tatrichter bei der Schätzung des Schadens insbesondere die etwaige Sensibilität der konkret betroffenen personenbezogenen Daten (vgl. Art. 9 Abs. 1 DSGVO) und deren typischerweise zweckgemäße Verwendung zu berücksichtigen.

Äußerst zweifelhaft erscheint daher, ob hier eine Festsetzung in 'gegebenenfalls nur einstelliger Höhe' mit dem Effektivitätsgrundsatz zu vereinbaren wäre (so aber obiter OLG Celle, Urteil vom 4. April 2024 - 5 U 31/23, juris Rn. 102). Dagegen hätte der Senat von Rechts wegen keine Bedenken, den notwendigen Ausgleich für den eingetretenen Kontrollverlust als solchem in einem Fall wie dem streitgegenständlichen in einer Größenordnung von 100 € (so obiter OLG Hamm, GRUR-RS 2024, 16856 Rn. 40) zu bemessen.

case_law.verification_method: OLDP full-text decision retrieved; ECLI matches the ECLI displayed at bundesgerichtshof.de press release Nr. 218/2024; later ruling VI ZR 375/24 (12.5.2026) at bundesgerichtshof.de explicitly cites 'BGHZ 242, 180' and quotes the same Rn. regarding Art. 82 DSGVO; third-party legal literature (recht.dfn.de Infobrief 3/2025) cites the same decision with identical ECLI.
case_law.later_history: Wird in dejure.org (Stand 2026-07-30) von 235 Folgerechtsprechungen zitiert. Wird in BGH, Urt. v. 12.5.2026 – VI ZR 375/24 ausdrücklich als BGHZ 242, 180 zitiert.
case_law.recommended_use: Anchors the German national rule for the quantum of non-material damages under Art. 82(1) DSGVO when only a temporary loss of control over personal data is established; provides a ~100 € indicative amount for purely control-loss cases.
cautions: Decision binds lower courts as revisional highest-instance interpretation; for EU-law conformity the underlying CJEU precedent (Österreichische Post C-300/21; Scalable Capital C-182/22) controls.
The 100 € figure is the BGH's obiter indication for the case before it (Facebook scraping, narrow Kontrollverlust); it is not a tariff and is not binding on Tatrichter within § 287 ZPO.
Decision does not address Art. 22 DSGVO or Art. 15 DSGVO recipients separately; those clusters require different German anchors.

case_law.decision_name: Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Limited and Maximillian Schrems

citation.full: Court of Justice of the European Union, Judgment of 16 July 2020, Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Limited and Schrems, Case C-311/18, ECLI:EU:C:2020:559.

case_law.procedural_posture: preliminary ruling (Article 267 TFEU); reference from the High Court (Ireland), decision of 4 May 2018, received at the Court on 9 May 2018
case_law.composition: Grand Chamber (President K. Lenaerts, Vice-President R. Silva de Lapuerta, Presidents of Chambers A. Arabadjiev, A. Prechal, M. Vilaras, M. Safjan, S. Rodin, Judges T. von Danwitz, F. Biltgen, etc.)
case_law.holding: On a reference from the High Court of Ireland, the Grand Chamber: (1) interpreted Article 2(1) and (2) GDPR to apply to transfers of personal data for commercial purposes by an EU-established economic operator to a third-country economic operator irrespective of subsequent public-authority processing for national-security purposes; (2) interpreted Article 46(1) and 46(2)(c) GDPR to require that the appropriate safeguards, enforceable rights and effective legal remedies ensure a level of protection essentially equivalent to that guaranteed by the GDPR read with the Charter, taking into account both contractual clauses and the legal system of the third country regarding public-authority access; (3) interpreted Article 58(2)(f) and (j) GDPR to require the competent supervisory authority to suspend or prohibit a transfer pursuant to standard data protection clauses where those clauses are not or cannot be complied with in the third country and the EU-law level of protection cannot be ensured by other means, unless a valid adequacy decision exists; (4) upheld the validity of Commission Decision 2010/87/EU (SCC Decision) as amended by Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/2297; (5) declared Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 (EU-US Privacy Shield) invalid.

holding_per_operative_item.1: Article 2(1) and (2) GDPR — applies to commercial transfers to a third-country operator irrespective of subsequent public-authority processing for national-security purposes.
holding_per_operative_item.2: Article 46(1) and 46(2)(c) GDPR — appropriate safeguards must ensure essentially equivalent protection; assessment must consider both contractual clauses and the third-country legal system, including the Article 45(2) non-exhaustive factors.
holding_per_operative_item.3: Article 58(2)(f) and (j) GDPR — supervisory authority must suspend or prohibit a transfer under SCCs where (a) no valid adequacy decision exists, (b) the clauses are not or cannot be complied with, (c) the EU-law level of protection cannot be ensured by other means, and (d) the controller/processor has not itself suspended or ended the transfer.
holding_per_operative_item.4: Decision 2010/87/EU (SCC Decision), as amended by Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/2297, examined in the light of Articles 7, 8 and 47 of the Charter — validity disclosed nothing to affect it; upheld.
holding_per_operative_item.5: Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 (EU-US Privacy Shield) — invalid; the Commission's finding that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection disregarded the requirements of Article 45(3) GDPR read with Articles 7, 8 and 47 of the Charter.

case_law.later_history: Privacy Shield was replaced by the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795 of 10 July 2023) — not addressed in the present artifact (out of cluster scope). case_law.holding: Article 15(1)(c) GDPR generally requires the controller, when personal data have been or will be disclosed, to provide the actual identity of the recipients. Categories alone suffice only where specific recipients cannot be identified, including where they are not yet known, or where the controller proves that the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive under Article 12(5) GDPR.
case_law.later_history: Final Court of Justice preliminary ruling; no ordinary appeal lies against the judgment.

case_law.court: Court of Justice of the European Union (Third Chamber)

citation.full: Judgment of the Court (Third Chamber) of 4 May 2023, UI v Österreichische Post AG, C-300/21, ECLI:EU:C:2023:370
citation.pinpoint: operative part points 1, 2 and 3 and reasoning paragraphs 30, 32, 42, 44, 46, 50, 51, 58 and 59

case_law.authority: binding preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU
case_law.procedural_posture: Reference for a preliminary ruling from the Oberster Gerichtshof (Supreme Court, Austria) in proceedings between UI and the Austrian postal operator about compensation for non-material damage following unlawful processing of political-affinity data.
bounded_holding: Article 82(1) GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the mere infringement of the GDPR is not sufficient to confer a right to compensation; the data subject must show actual (material or non-material) damage, an infringement of the GDPR, and a causal link between the two — those three conditions are cumulative (paragraphs 31–32, 42, operative point 1).
Article 82(1) GDPR precludes a national rule or practice making compensation for non-material damage subject to a threshold of seriousness (paragraphs 44–46, 50–51, operative point 2).

In the absence of EU rules on quantification, the amount of damages is governed by national law but must comply with the principles of equivalence and effectiveness, and must be 'full and effective' (sixth sentence of recital 146 GDPR) without being punitive (paragraphs 53, 56–58, operative point 3).
case_law.later_history: No review or appeal affects this judgment. Affirmed and applied by the Court in Case C-340/21 (VB v NAP), paragraphs 77 and 78, on the three cumulative conditions and the no-threshold rule.

The judgment thereby interprets Article 82(3) by reference to the strict-cumulative-condition framework that the exemption must overcome.
outbound_relations.holding: Article 82(3) GDPR must be read together with Article 82(1) and (2): the controller's exemption is conditional on affirmatively proving that it is not in any way responsible for the damage, consistent with the cumulative-condition framework.

case_law.decision_name: Meta Platforms Inc and Others v Bundeskartellamt

citation.full: Court of Justice of the European Union, Judgment of 4 July 2023, Meta Platforms Inc and Others v Bundeskartellamt, Case C-252/21, ECLI:EU:C:2023:537.

case_law.procedural_posture: preliminary ruling (Article 267 TFEU); reference from Oberlandesgericht Düsseldorf (Higher Regional Court, Düsseldorf, Germany), decision of 24 March 2021, received at the Court on 22 April 2021
case_law.language: de (language of the case); EN authentic rendition used for verification
case_law.composition: Grand Chamber (President K. Lenaerts, Vice-President L. Bay Larsen, Presidents of Chambers A. Prechal, K. Jürimäe, C. Lycourgos, M. Safjan, L.S. Rossi (Rapporteur), D. Gratsias, M.L. Arastey Sahún, Judges J.-C. Bonichot, S. Rodin, F. Biltgen)
case_law.holding: On a reference from the Oberlandesgericht Düsseldorf, the Grand Chamber ruled that: (1) Article 51 et seq. GDPR and Article 4(3) TEU permit a national competition authority, when applying Article 102 TFEU, to find that an undertaking's general terms of use concerning personal-data processing are inconsistent with the GDPR, subject to the duty of sincere cooperation with the supervisory authorities; (2) Article 9(1) GDPR covers the collection of special-category data via cookies/integrated interfaces on third-party sites/apps where this reveals information falling within Article 9(1); (3) Article 9(2)(e) GDPR is not satisfied merely by visiting such sites/apps — the user must have explicitly chosen, by full-knowledge individual settings, to make the data publicly accessible to an unlimited audience; (4) Article 6(1)(b) GDPR requires that processing be objectively indispensable for a purpose integral to the contractual obligation such that the main subject matter of the contract cannot be achieved without it; (5) Article 6(1)(f) GDPR requires informed notice of the legitimate interest, strict necessity, and a balancing showing that the user's interests do not override; (6) Article 6(1)(c) GDPR is available where the legal basis meets an objective of public interest and is proportionate and strictly necessary; (7) Article 6(1)(d) and (e) GDPR in principle cannot justify the cross-service data combination at issue; (8) Article 6(1)(a) and Article 9(2)(a) GDPR read with the Article 4(11) definition of consent — a dominant position does not, as such, preclude valid consent, but is an important factor for assessing whether consent was freely given.

holding_per_operative_item.1: Article 51 et seq. GDPR + Article 4(3) TEU — competition authority may find inconsistency with GDPR; duty of sincere cooperation with supervisory authorities; cannot depart from a competent supervisory-authority decision.
holding_per_operative_item.2: Article 9(1) GDPR — collection via integrated interfaces/cookies on third-party sites/apps, linking to the social-network account, is 'processing of special categories of personal data' under Article 9(1) where it reveals information within those categories.
holding_per_operative_item.3: Article 9(2)(e) GDPR — visiting such sites/apps does not constitute manifestly making public; explicit prior individual choice is required for the data entered or resulting from clicks to be 'manifestly made public'.
holding_per_operative_item.4: Article 6(1)(b) GDPR — 'necessary for performance of a contract' requires objective indispensability for a purpose integral to the contractual obligation; without the processing the main subject matter of the contract cannot be achieved.
holding_per_operative_item.5: Article 6(1)(f) GDPR — 'necessary for legitimate interests' requires (i) informed notice of the legitimate interest, (ii) strict necessity, and (iii) a balancing showing that the data subject's interests/freedoms do not override.
holding_per_operative_item.6: Article 6(1)(c) GDPR — 'necessary for compliance with a legal obligation' available only where the legal basis pursues an objective of public interest, is proportionate to the legitimate aim, and the processing is strictly necessary.
holding_per_operative_item.7: Article 6(1)(d) and (e) GDPR — vital-interests (d) and public-interest/official-authority (e) bases, in principle and subject to verification, cannot justify the cross-service processing described.
holding_per_operative_item.8: Article 6(1)(a) and Article 9(2)(a) GDPR + Article 4(11) — dominant position does not, as such, preclude valid consent, but is an important factor for the freely-given condition; the operator bears the burden of proof.

case_law.later_history: No further EU proceedings identified within the cutoff date (2026-07-30); referenced in subsequent CJEU and national-court decisions. Confirmed via lex_cited_by(32016R0679) inbound network (462 inbound reference edges to GDPR recorded).

case_law.court: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber)
case_law.decision_name: Deutsche Wohnen SE v Staatsanwaltschaft Berlin
case_law.author: Court of Justice
case_law.referring_court: Kammergericht Berlin (Higher Regional Court, Berlin, Germany)
case_law.publication_status: Published in the digital reports of cases with official status (EUR-Lex).

citation.full: EuGH (Grand Chamber), Urt. v. 5.12.2023 – C-807/21 –, ECLI:EU:C:2023:950, Rn. 39-78, operative rulings 1-2 – Deutsche Wohnen SE v Staatsanwaltschaft Berlin.

questions_referred: Q1 (rephrased): Whether Article 58(2) and Article 83(1) to (6) of the GDPR preclude national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person.

Q2 (rephrased): Whether Article 83 of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that an administrative fine may be imposed pursuant to that provision only where it is established that the controller, which is both a legal person and an undertaking, intentionally or negligently committed an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) of the GDPR.
case_law.holding: The Court (Grand Chamber) holds: (1) Article 58(2)(i) and Article 83(1) to (6) of the GDPR must be interpreted as precluding national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person; (2) Article 83 of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that an administrative fine may be imposed pursuant to that provision only where it is established that the controller, which is both a legal person and an undertaking, intentionally or negligently committed an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) thereof.

operative_clauses.text: Article 58(2)(i) and Article 83(1) to (6) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), must be interpreted as precluding national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person.

Article 83 of Regulation 2016/679 must be interpreted as meaning that an administrative fine may be imposed pursuant to that provision only where it is established that the controller, which is both a legal person and an undertaking, intentionally or negligently committed an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) thereof.

case_law.facts_summary: The Berlin data protection supervisory authority imposed an administrative fine of EUR 14,385,000 on Deutsche Wohnen SE (DW) for intentional infringement of Article 5(1)(a), (c) and (e) and Article 25(1) of the GDPR (storage of tenant personal data that was no longer necessary). The Landgericht Berlin (Regional Court) annulled the decision, holding that under German law (Paragraph 30 of the OWiG, applied via Paragraph 41(1) of the Bundesdatenschutzgesetz) a fine may be imposed on a legal person only where an administrative offence has first been attributed to an identified natural person acting as a representative of the legal person. The Kammergericht Berlin (Higher Regional Court) referred two questions to the CJEU: (Q1) whether Art 83 GDPR permits direct fines on legal persons without prior identification of a natural person; (Q2) whether fines require intentional or negligent conduct.
case_law.later_history: Subsequent GDPR case law has cited Deutsche Wohnen as authority on Article 4(7) (controller concept) and Article 83(4) to (6) (fines on legal persons, fault requirement). Cited inter alia by: État belge v Autorité de protection des données (C-231/22, judgment 11 January 2024) on Article 4(7); ILVA A/S (C-383/23, judgment 13 February 2025) on Article 83(4) to (6) and (9) and the concept of 'undertaking'; Amt der Tiroler Landesregierung v Datenschutzbehörde (C-638/23, judgment 27 February 2025) on Article 4(7). No appeal or review of the Deutsche Wohnen judgment was identified; it is final.

This is recorded as an interpretation of Article 4 (subunit (7)) within the existing article-Art4-Para1 block (the definition article has only one canonical paragraph node in the GDPR base graph; sub-unit (7) is captured in akn4eu_sub_units).
outbound_relations.holding: Article 4(7) of the GDPR defines the concept of 'controller' broadly, as referring to the natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data. The EU legislature did not distinguish, for the purposes of determining liability under that regulation, between natural persons and legal persons, that liability being subject to the sole condition that those persons, alone or jointly with others, determine the purposes and means of processing of personal data.

outbound_relations.reasoning: Paragraphs 45-47, 51, 71 and operative ruling 1 interpret Article 58(2) GDPR (specifically Article 58(2)(i)). The Court holds that Article 58(2) sets out the supervisory authorities' corrective powers in detail, without referring to Member-State law or leaving discretion, and that the power under Article 58(2)(i) to impose an administrative fine may be exercised directly against a legal person acting as controller, without prior identification of a natural person. The Member State may regulate the procedure but may not impose substantive conditions beyond Article 83(1) to (6).
outbound_relations.holding: It follows from a combined reading of Article 4(7), Article 83 and Article 58(2)(i) of the GDPR that an administrative fine in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) may also be imposed on legal persons where they are controllers. No provision of the GDPR permits the inference that the imposition of an administrative fine on a legal person as a controller is subject to a previous finding that that infringement was committed by an identified natural person.

Article 83(4) is one of the specific tiers whose substantive conditions the Court construes; accordingly, the judgment is mapped to article-Art83-Para4 as part of the operative ruling that Article 83(1) to (6) precludes national attribution-to-natural-person requirements.
