holding.bounded_holding: Article 22(1) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value based on personal data relating to a person and concerning his or her ability to meet payment commitments in the future constitutes 'automated individual decision-making' within the meaning of that provision, where a third party, to which that probability value is transmitted, draws strongly on that probability value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.

doctrinal_components.point: Three cumulative conditions for Article 22(1) (decision; based solely on automated processing including profiling; legal effects or similarly significant effect)
The concept of 'decision' in Article 22(1) is broad and can encompass the result of calculating a person's creditworthiness in the form of a probability value
Scoring by SCHUFA meets the definition of 'profiling' in Article 4(4) of the GDPR (cumulative condition two is met)
Where the third party draws 'strongly' on the probability value, the third cumulative condition (legal effects or similarly significantly affects) is fulfilled
The probability value itself, in such circumstances, must be qualified as a decision producing legal effects or similarly significantly affecting the data subject within the meaning of Article 22(1)
A restrictive interpretation limited to the act of the third party would create a lacuna in legal protection and a risk of circumvention of Article 22

Member-State law authorising automated decision-making under Article 22(2)(b) must comply with Articles 5 and 6 of the GDPR; Member States are not empowered to add substantive lawfulness conditions beyond Article 6(1)(c) and (e)

Article 15(1)(h) gives the data subject the right to obtain 'meaningful information about the logic involved' from the controller that establishes the probability value, lest the data subject be unable to access that information from any other party

verification_quotes.quote: The applicability of that provision is therefore subject to three cumulative conditions, namely, first, that there must be a 'decision', secondly, that that decision must be 'based solely on automated processing, including profiling', and, thirdly, that it must produce 'legal effects concerning [the interested party]' or 'similarly significantly [affect] him or her'.

The concept of 'decision' within the meaning of Article 22(1) of the GDPR is thus, as the Advocate General noted in point 38 of his Opinion, capable of including a number of acts which may affect the data subject in many ways, since that concept is broad enough to encompass the result of calculating a person's creditworthiness in the form of a probability value concerning that person's ability to meet payment commitments in the future.

As regards, secondly, the condition according to which the decision, within the meaning of that Article 22(1), must be 'based solely on automated processing, including profiling', as the Advocate General noted in point 33 of his Opinion, it is common ground that an activity such as that of SCHUFA meets the definition of 'profiling' appearing in Article 4(4) of the GDPR and therefore that that condition is met in the present case, since the wording of the first question referred explicitly refers to the automated establishment of a probability value based on personal data relating to a person and concerning that person's ability to repay a loan in the future.

As regards, thirdly, the condition that the decision must produce 'legal effects' concerning the person at issue or affect him or her 'similarly significantly', it is apparent from the very wording of the first question referred that the action of the third party to whom the probability value is transmitted draws 'strongly' on that value. Thus, according to the factual findings of the referring court, in the event where a loan application is sent by a consumer to a bank, an insufficient probability value leads, in almost all cases, to the refusal of that bank to grant the loan applied for.

It follows that, in circumstances such as those at issue in the main proceedings, in which the probability value established by a credit information agency and communicated to a bank plays a determining role in the granting of credit, the establishment of that value must be qualified in itself as a decision producing vis-à-vis a data subject 'legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly [affecting] him or her' within the meaning of Article 22(1) of the GDPR.

Furthermore, in the case of automated decision-making, such as that referred to in Article 22(1) of the GDPR, first, the controller is subject to additional information obligations under Article 13(2)(f) and Article 14(2)(g) of that regulation. Secondly, the data subject enjoys, under Article 15(1)(h) of that regulation, the right to obtain from the controller, in particular, 'meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject'.

Furthermore, as the Advocate General noted in point 48 of his Opinion, first, the data subject would not be able to assert, from the credit information agency which establishes the probability value concerning him or her, his or her right of access to the specific information referred to in Article 15(1)(h) of the GDPR, in the absence of automated decision-making by that company. Secondly, even assuming that the act adopted by the third party falls within the scope of Article 22(1) of that regulation in so far as it fulfils the conditions for application of that provision, that third party would not be able to provide that specific information because it generally does not have it.

The fact that the establishment of a probability value such as that at issue in the main proceedings is covered by Article 22(1) of the GDPR has the consequence, as noted in paragraphs 53 to 55 of this judgment, that it is prohibited unless one of the exceptions set out in Article 22(2) of that regulation is applicable and the specific requirements provided for in Article 22(3) and (4) of that regulation are complied with.

Thus, in the event that the law of a Member State authorises, under Article 22(2)(b) of the GDPR, the adoption of a decision solely based on automated processing, that processing must comply not only with the conditions set out in the latter provision and in Article 22(4) of that regulation, but also with the requirements set out in Articles 5 and 6 of that regulation. Accordingly, Member States cannot adopt, under Article 22(2)(b) of the GDPR, regulations which authorise profiling in disregard of the requirements laid down by those Articles 5 and 6, as interpreted by the case-law of the Court.

Article 22(1) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value based on personal data relating to a person and concerning his or her ability to meet payment commitments in the future constitutes 'automated individual decision-making' within the meaning of that provision, where a third party, to which that probability value is transmitted, draws strongly on that probability value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.

Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 ... must be interpreted as meaning that the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value based on personal data relating to a person and concerning his or her ability to meet payment commitments in the future constitutes 'automated individual decision-making' within the meaning of that provision, where a third party, to which that probability value is transmitted, draws strongly on that probability value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.

outbound_relations.reasoning: The Court expressly interprets Article 22(1) GDPR as covering the automated establishment of a probability value (scoring) by a credit information agency where a third party draws strongly on that value. This is the principal holding of the judgment and constrains the meaning of the 'decision' element in Article 22(1).
outbound_relations.holding: Article 22(1) GDPR covers the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value concerning a person's ability to meet payment commitments in the future, where a third party draws strongly on that value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.

outbound_relations.reasoning: The holding directs national courts to assess whether Member-State law (e.g. Paragraph 31 BDSG) can serve as a legal basis under Article 22(2)(b) GDPR for automated scoring; the judgment sets out the conditions of lawful authorisation under Article 22(2)(b) and explains how Article 22(2) interacts with Articles 5 and 6 GDPR (paragraphs 65-69).
outbound_relations.holding: Article 22(2)(b) GDPR requires the Member-State law authorising automated individual decision-making to lay down suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and legitimate interests; that law must comply with Articles 5 and 6 GDPR, and Member States are not empowered to add substantive lawfulness rules beyond Article 6(1)(c) and (e).

outbound_relations.reasoning: The Court explicitly affirms (paragraph 66) that the suitable measures required under Article 22(2)(b) and, a fortiori, the safeguards under Article 22(3) include 'at least the right for the data subject to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express his or her point of view and to challenge the decision'; this is a direct interpretation of the safeguards enumerated in Article 22(3).
outbound_relations.holding: Article 22(3) GDPR safeguards (human intervention, expression of point of view, contestation) are integral to any automated decision-making falling within Article 22(1), including scoring by a credit information agency.

outbound_relations.reasoning: The Court holds (paragraph 56, restated in paragraph 63) that the data subject enjoys the right under Article 15(1)(h) GDPR to obtain from the controller that establishes the probability value 'meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing'; without this, the right of access would be hollowed out, as the third-party recipient does not have that information. This is a binding interpretation of Article 15(1)(h), which is part of Article 15(1).
outbound_relations.holding: Article 15(1)(h) GDPR requires the controller that establishes the creditworthiness probability value to disclose meaningful information about the logic involved, the significance and the envisaged consequences of the automated decision-making, lest the data subject's right of access become ineffective in a multi-stakeholder scoring scenario.

case_law.authority: binding preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU
case_law.procedural_posture: Reference for a preliminary ruling from the Varhoven administrativen sad (Supreme Administrative Court, Bulgaria) in proceedings brought by an individual affected by the 2019 cyberattack on the Bulgarian National Revenue Agency, seeking non-material damage compensation under Article 82 GDPR.
bounded_holding: Articles 24 and 32 GDPR: unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data by a third party is not sufficient, in itself, to presume that the technical and organisational measures implemented by the controller were not appropriate (paragraphs 31–39, operative point 1).

Article 32 GDPR: the appropriateness of the technical and organisational measures must be assessed by the national courts in a concrete manner, taking into account the risks of the processing and the nature, content and implementation of the measures (paragraphs 42–47, operative point 2).

Article 5(2) read with Article 24 GDPR: in an Article 82 action, the controller bears the burden of proving that the security measures implemented by it are appropriate under Article 32 (paragraphs 49–57, operative point 3).

Article 32 GDPR and the principle of effectiveness: an expert's report cannot constitute a systematically necessary and sufficient means of proof of the appropriateness of the security measures (paragraphs 58–64, operative point 4).

Article 82(3) GDPR: the controller cannot be exempt from compensation under Article 82(1) and (2) solely because the damage is the result of unauthorised access by a third party; the controller must then prove that it is in no way responsible for the event giving rise to the damage (paragraphs 65–74, operative point 5).

Article 82(1) GDPR: the fear experienced by a data subject that his or her personal data might be misused in the future as a result of an infringement of the GDPR is capable, in itself, of constituting 'non-material damage' within the meaning of that provision (paragraphs 75–86, operative point 6).
case_law.later_history: No review or appeal affects this judgment. Builds on and applies the holdings of Case C-300/21 (UI v Österreichische Post) as confirmed authority for the three cumulative conditions and the no-threshold rule (paragraphs 77–78).

judgments.interpretation_issue: Höhe des immateriellen Schadensersatzes nach Art. 82 Abs. 1 DSGVO bei kurzzeitigem Kontrollverlust über eigene personenbezogene Daten (Facebook-Scraping-Vorfall).
judgments.holding: Bei einem bloßen Kontrollverlust über personenbezogene Daten ohne darüber hinausgehende psychische Beeinträchtigung hält der Senat eine Entschädigung in einer Größenordnung von 100 € als mit dem Effektivitätsgrundsatz vereinbar; eine Festsetzung in 'gegebenenfalls nur einstelliger Höhe' ist äußerst zweifelhaft. Schadensersatz nach Art. 82 Abs. 1 DSGVO darf weder hinter dem vollständigen Ausgleich zurückbleiben noch über ihn hinausgehen.
reasoning: Tatrichter hat bei Schätzung nach § 287 ZPO die Sensibilität der Daten (Art. 9 Abs. 1 DSGVO), Art des Kontrollverlusts (begrenzter/unbegrenzter Empfängerkreis), Dauer und Möglichkeit der Wiedererlangung der Kontrolle zu berücksichtigen (Rn. 99).

Senat schließt sich ausdrücklich der EuGH-Linie an, dass der immaterielle Schaden nicht weniger schwer wiegt als bei einer Körperverletzung (Rn. 97, unter Verweis auf EuGH C-200/23 Rn. 151 und C-182/22 Rn. 39 – Scalable Capital).
Bei bloßem Kontrollverlust indiziert der Senat 100 € als effektiven Ausgleich und lehnt OLG Celle (5 U 31/23 Rn. 102) als obiter abweichende Bemessung ab (Rn. 100).

pinpoints.quote_verbatim: Ist nach den Feststellungen des Gerichts allein ein Schaden in Form eines Kontrollverlusts an personenbezogenen Daten gegeben, weil weitere Schäden nicht nachgewiesen sind, hat der Tatrichter bei der Schätzung des Schadens insbesondere die etwaige Sensibilität der konkret betroffenen personenbezogenen Daten (vgl. Art. 9 Abs. 1 DSGVO) und deren typischerweise zweckgemäße Verwendung zu berücksichtigen.

Äußerst zweifelhaft erscheint daher, ob hier eine Festsetzung in 'gegebenenfalls nur einstelliger Höhe' mit dem Effektivitätsgrundsatz zu vereinbaren wäre (so aber obiter OLG Celle, Urteil vom 4. April 2024 - 5 U 31/23, juris Rn. 102). Dagegen hätte der Senat von Rechts wegen keine Bedenken, den notwendigen Ausgleich für den eingetretenen Kontrollverlust als solchem in einem Fall wie dem streitgegenständlichen in einer Größenordnung von 100 € (so obiter OLG Hamm, GRUR-RS 2024, 16856 Rn. 40) zu bemessen.

judgments.procedural_posture: preliminary ruling (Article 267 TFEU); reference from the High Court (Ireland), decision of 4 May 2018, received at the Court on 9 May 2018
judgments.composition: Grand Chamber (President K. Lenaerts, Vice-President R. Silva de Lapuerta, Presidents of Chambers A. Arabadjiev, A. Prechal, M. Vilaras, M. Safjan, S. Rodin, Judges T. von Danwitz, F. Biltgen, etc.)
judgments.holding: On a reference from the High Court of Ireland, the Grand Chamber: (1) interpreted Article 2(1) and (2) GDPR to apply to transfers of personal data for commercial purposes by an EU-established economic operator to a third-country economic operator irrespective of subsequent public-authority processing for national-security purposes; (2) interpreted Article 46(1) and 46(2)(c) GDPR to require that the appropriate safeguards, enforceable rights and effective legal remedies ensure a level of protection essentially equivalent to that guaranteed by the GDPR read with the Charter, taking into account both contractual clauses and the legal system of the third country regarding public-authority access; (3) interpreted Article 58(2)(f) and (j) GDPR to require the competent supervisory authority to suspend or prohibit a transfer pursuant to standard data protection clauses where those clauses are not or cannot be complied with in the third country and the EU-law level of protection cannot be ensured by other means, unless a valid adequacy decision exists; (4) upheld the validity of Commission Decision 2010/87/EU (SCC Decision) as amended by Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/2297; (5) declared Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 (EU-US Privacy Shield) invalid.

holding_per_operative_item.1: Article 2(1) and (2) GDPR — applies to commercial transfers to a third-country operator irrespective of subsequent public-authority processing for national-security purposes.
holding_per_operative_item.2: Article 46(1) and 46(2)(c) GDPR — appropriate safeguards must ensure essentially equivalent protection; assessment must consider both contractual clauses and the third-country legal system, including the Article 45(2) non-exhaustive factors.
holding_per_operative_item.3: Article 58(2)(f) and (j) GDPR — supervisory authority must suspend or prohibit a transfer under SCCs where (a) no valid adequacy decision exists, (b) the clauses are not or cannot be complied with, (c) the EU-law level of protection cannot be ensured by other means, and (d) the controller/processor has not itself suspended or ended the transfer.
holding_per_operative_item.4: Decision 2010/87/EU (SCC Decision), as amended by Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/2297, examined in the light of Articles 7, 8 and 47 of the Charter — validity disclosed nothing to affect it; upheld.
holding_per_operative_item.5: Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 (EU-US Privacy Shield) — invalid; the Commission's finding that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection disregarded the requirements of Article 45(3) GDPR read with Articles 7, 8 and 47 of the Charter.

judgments.procedural_posture: Reference for a preliminary ruling from the Oberster Gerichtshof (Supreme Court, Austria) in proceedings between UI and the Austrian postal operator about compensation for non-material damage following unlawful processing of political-affinity data.
bounded_holding: Article 82(1) GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the mere infringement of the GDPR is not sufficient to confer a right to compensation; the data subject must show actual (material or non-material) damage, an infringement of the GDPR, and a causal link between the two — those three conditions are cumulative (paragraphs 31–32, 42, operative point 1).
Article 82(1) GDPR precludes a national rule or practice making compensation for non-material damage subject to a threshold of seriousness (paragraphs 44–46, 50–51, operative point 2).

In the absence of EU rules on quantification, the amount of damages is governed by national law but must comply with the principles of equivalence and effectiveness, and must be 'full and effective' (sixth sentence of recital 146 GDPR) without being punitive (paragraphs 53, 56–58, operative point 3).
judgments.later_history: No review or appeal affects this judgment. Affirmed and applied by the Court in Case C-340/21 (VB v NAP), paragraphs 77 and 78, on the three cumulative conditions and the no-threshold rule.

judgments.procedural_posture: preliminary ruling (Article 267 TFEU); reference from Oberlandesgericht Düsseldorf (Higher Regional Court, Düsseldorf, Germany), decision of 24 March 2021, received at the Court on 22 April 2021

judgments.holding: On a reference from the Oberlandesgericht Düsseldorf, the Grand Chamber ruled that: (1) Article 51 et seq. GDPR and Article 4(3) TEU permit a national competition authority, when applying Article 102 TFEU, to find that an undertaking's general terms of use concerning personal-data processing are inconsistent with the GDPR, subject to the duty of sincere cooperation with the supervisory authorities; (2) Article 9(1) GDPR covers the collection of special-category data via cookies/integrated interfaces on third-party sites/apps where this reveals information falling within Article 9(1); (3) Article 9(2)(e) GDPR is not satisfied merely by visiting such sites/apps — the user must have explicitly chosen, by full-knowledge individual settings, to make the data publicly accessible to an unlimited audience; (4) Article 6(1)(b) GDPR requires that processing be objectively indispensable for a purpose integral to the contractual obligation such that the main subject matter of the contract cannot be achieved without it; (5) Article 6(1)(f) GDPR requires informed notice of the legitimate interest, strict necessity, and a balancing showing that the user's interests do not override; (6) Article 6(1)(c) GDPR is available where the legal basis meets an objective of public interest and is proportionate and strictly necessary; (7) Article 6(1)(d) and (e) GDPR in principle cannot justify the cross-service data combination at issue; (8) Article 6(1)(a) and Article 9(2)(a) GDPR read with the Article 4(11) definition of consent — a dominant position does not, as such, preclude valid consent, but is an important factor for assessing whether consent was freely given.

holding_per_operative_item.1: Article 51 et seq. GDPR + Article 4(3) TEU — competition authority may find inconsistency with GDPR; duty of sincere cooperation with supervisory authorities; cannot depart from a competent supervisory-authority decision.
holding_per_operative_item.2: Article 9(1) GDPR — collection via integrated interfaces/cookies on third-party sites/apps, linking to the social-network account, is 'processing of special categories of personal data' under Article 9(1) where it reveals information within those categories.
holding_per_operative_item.3: Article 9(2)(e) GDPR — visiting such sites/apps does not constitute manifestly making public; explicit prior individual choice is required for the data entered or resulting from clicks to be 'manifestly made public'.
holding_per_operative_item.4: Article 6(1)(b) GDPR — 'necessary for performance of a contract' requires objective indispensability for a purpose integral to the contractual obligation; without the processing the main subject matter of the contract cannot be achieved.
holding_per_operative_item.5: Article 6(1)(f) GDPR — 'necessary for legitimate interests' requires (i) informed notice of the legitimate interest, (ii) strict necessity, and (iii) a balancing showing that the data subject's interests/freedoms do not override.
holding_per_operative_item.6: Article 6(1)(c) GDPR — 'necessary for compliance with a legal obligation' available only where the legal basis pursues an objective of public interest, is proportionate to the legitimate aim, and the processing is strictly necessary.
holding_per_operative_item.7: Article 6(1)(d) and (e) GDPR — vital-interests (d) and public-interest/official-authority (e) bases, in principle and subject to verification, cannot justify the cross-service processing described.
holding_per_operative_item.8: Article 6(1)(a) and Article 9(2)(a) GDPR + Article 4(11) — dominant position does not, as such, preclude valid consent, but is an important factor for the freely-given condition; the operator bears the burden of proof.

citation.full: EuGH (Grand Chamber), Urt. v. 5.12.2023 – C-807/21 –, ECLI:EU:C:2023:950, Rn. 39-78, operative rulings 1-2 – Deutsche Wohnen SE v Staatsanwaltschaft Berlin.

questions_referred: Q1 (rephrased): Whether Article 58(2) and Article 83(1) to (6) of the GDPR preclude national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person.

Q2 (rephrased): Whether Article 83 of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that an administrative fine may be imposed pursuant to that provision only where it is established that the controller, which is both a legal person and an undertaking, intentionally or negligently committed an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) of the GDPR.
judgments.holding: The Court (Grand Chamber) holds: (1) Article 58(2)(i) and Article 83(1) to (6) of the GDPR must be interpreted as precluding national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person; (2) Article 83 of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that an administrative fine may be imposed pursuant to that provision only where it is established that the controller, which is both a legal person and an undertaking, intentionally or negligently committed an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) thereof.

operative_clauses.text: Article 58(2)(i) and Article 83(1) to (6) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation), must be interpreted as precluding national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person.

Article 83 of Regulation 2016/679 must be interpreted as meaning that an administrative fine may be imposed pursuant to that provision only where it is established that the controller, which is both a legal person and an undertaking, intentionally or negligently committed an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) thereof.

judgments.facts_summary: The Berlin data protection supervisory authority imposed an administrative fine of EUR 14,385,000 on Deutsche Wohnen SE (DW) for intentional infringement of Article 5(1)(a), (c) and (e) and Article 25(1) of the GDPR (storage of tenant personal data that was no longer necessary). The Landgericht Berlin (Regional Court) annulled the decision, holding that under German law (Paragraph 30 of the OWiG, applied via Paragraph 41(1) of the Bundesdatenschutzgesetz) a fine may be imposed on a legal person only where an administrative offence has first been attributed to an identified natural person acting as a representative of the legal person. The Kammergericht Berlin (Higher Regional Court) referred two questions to the CJEU: (Q1) whether Art 83 GDPR permits direct fines on legal persons without prior identification of a natural person; (Q2) whether fines require intentional or negligent conduct.
judgments.later_history: Subsequent GDPR case law has cited Deutsche Wohnen as authority on Article 4(7) (controller concept) and Article 83(4) to (6) (fines on legal persons, fault requirement). Cited inter alia by: État belge v Autorité de protection des données (C-231/22, judgment 11 January 2024) on Article 4(7); ILVA A/S (C-383/23, judgment 13 February 2025) on Article 83(4) to (6) and (9) and the concept of 'undertaking'; Amt der Tiroler Landesregierung v Datenschutzbehörde (C-638/23, judgment 27 February 2025) on Article 4(7). No appeal or review of the Deutsche Wohnen judgment was identified; it is final.

This is recorded as an interpretation of Article 4 (subunit (7)) within the existing article-Art4-Para1 block (the definition article has only one canonical paragraph node in the GDPR base graph; sub-unit (7) is captured in akn4eu_sub_units).
outbound_relations.holding: Article 4(7) of the GDPR defines the concept of 'controller' broadly, as referring to the natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data. The EU legislature did not distinguish, for the purposes of determining liability under that regulation, between natural persons and legal persons, that liability being subject to the sole condition that those persons, alone or jointly with others, determine the purposes and means of processing of personal data.

outbound_relations.reasoning: Paragraphs 45-47, 51, 71 and operative ruling 1 interpret Article 58(2) GDPR (specifically Article 58(2)(i)). The Court holds that Article 58(2) sets out the supervisory authorities' corrective powers in detail, without referring to Member-State law or leaving discretion, and that the power under Article 58(2)(i) to impose an administrative fine may be exercised directly against a legal person acting as controller, without prior identification of a natural person. The Member State may regulate the procedure but may not impose substantive conditions beyond Article 83(1) to (6).
outbound_relations.holding: It follows from a combined reading of Article 4(7), Article 83 and Article 58(2)(i) of the GDPR that an administrative fine in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) may also be imposed on legal persons where they are controllers. No provision of the GDPR permits the inference that the imposition of an administrative fine on a legal person as a controller is subject to a previous finding that that infringement was committed by an identified natural person.

outbound_relations.reasoning: Paragraphs 60, 65, 75, 78 and operative rulings 1 and 2 interpret Article 83(1) to (6) of the GDPR collectively, including Article 83(4) as the first of the three graduated infringement tiers. The Court holds that the substantive conditions for fines in Article 83(4) to (6) are exhaustively governed by EU law and that fines under any of those tiers are precluded from being conditioned on prior attribution to an identified natural person. Article 83(4) is one of the specific tiers whose substantive conditions the Court construes; accordingly, the judgment is mapped to article-Art83-Para4 as part of the operative ruling that Article 83(1) to (6) precludes national attribution-to-natural-person requirements.
outbound_relations.holding: Article 83(4) to (6) of the GDPR must be interpreted as precluding national legislation under which an administrative fine may be imposed on a legal person in its capacity as controller in respect of an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) only in so far as that infringement has previously been attributed to an identified natural person; and as meaning that an administrative fine may be imposed pursuant to Article 83 only where it is established that the controller, which is both a legal person and an undertaking, intentionally or negligently committed an infringement referred to in Article 83(4) to (6) thereof.

outbound_relations.reasoning: The same operative holdings (paragraphs 60, 65, 75, 78; operative rulings 1 and 2) interpret Article 83(1) to (6) collectively, including Article 83(5) as the second graduated infringement tier. The ruling that substantive conditions for fines (fault requirement, no Member-State substantive additions) are exhaustively governed by EU law applies equally to Article 83(5).
outbound_relations.holding: Article 83(5) is part of the range exhaustively regulated by Article 83(1) to (6) GDPR; the same interpretation (no prior attribution to natural person; intentional or negligent infringement required) applies to fines imposed under that tier.

outbound_relations.reasoning: Paragraphs 60, 65, 75, 78 and operative rulings 1 and 2 interpret Article 83(1) to (6) collectively, including Article 83(6) (non-compliance with an order by the supervisory authority referred to in Article 58(2)). The same exhaustive-EU-law and fault-requirement holdings apply to fines under Article 83(6). In the present case, the underlying infringement under Article 83(4) to (6) was specifically identified in the referring court's question and the operative ruling expressly references 'Article 83(4) to (6)' as the infringement class the controller may be fined for; Article 83(6) is part of that range.
outbound_relations.holding: Article 83(6) is part of the range exhaustively regulated by Article 83(1) to (6) GDPR; fines under Article 83(6) for non-compliance with an Article 58(2) order against a legal-person controller are likewise subject to the same substantive conditions (no prior attribution to a natural person; intentional or negligent infringement required).

holding.bounded_holding: Article 22(1) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value based on personal data relating to a person and concerning his or her ability to meet payment commitments in the future constitutes 'automated individual decision-making' within the meaning of that provision, where a third party, to which that probability value is transmitted, draws strongly on that probability value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.

doctrinal_components.point: Three cumulative conditions for Article 22(1) (decision; based solely on automated processing including profiling; legal effects or similarly significant effect)
The concept of 'decision' in Article 22(1) is broad and can encompass the result of calculating a person's creditworthiness in the form of a probability value
Scoring by SCHUFA meets the definition of 'profiling' in Article 4(4) of the GDPR (cumulative condition two is met)
Where the third party draws 'strongly' on the probability value, the third cumulative condition (legal effects or similarly significantly affects) is fulfilled
The probability value itself, in such circumstances, must be qualified as a decision producing legal effects or similarly significantly affecting the data subject within the meaning of Article 22(1)
A restrictive interpretation limited to the act of the third party would create a lacuna in legal protection and a risk of circumvention of Article 22

Member-State law authorising automated decision-making under Article 22(2)(b) must comply with Articles 5 and 6 of the GDPR; Member States are not empowered to add substantive lawfulness conditions beyond Article 6(1)(c) and (e)

Article 15(1)(h) gives the data subject the right to obtain 'meaningful information about the logic involved' from the controller that establishes the probability value, lest the data subject be unable to access that information from any other party

verification_quotes.quote: The applicability of that provision is therefore subject to three cumulative conditions, namely, first, that there must be a 'decision', secondly, that that decision must be 'based solely on automated processing, including profiling', and, thirdly, that it must produce 'legal effects concerning [the interested party]' or 'similarly significantly [affect] him or her'.

The concept of 'decision' within the meaning of Article 22(1) of the GDPR is thus, as the Advocate General noted in point 38 of his Opinion, capable of including a number of acts which may affect the data subject in many ways, since that concept is broad enough to encompass the result of calculating a person's creditworthiness in the form of a probability value concerning that person's ability to meet payment commitments in the future.

As regards, secondly, the condition according to which the decision, within the meaning of that Article 22(1), must be 'based solely on automated processing, including profiling', as the Advocate General noted in point 33 of his Opinion, it is common ground that an activity such as that of SCHUFA meets the definition of 'profiling' appearing in Article 4(4) of the GDPR and therefore that that condition is met in the present case, since the wording of the first question referred explicitly refers to the automated establishment of a probability value based on personal data relating to a person and concerning that person's ability to repay a loan in the future.

As regards, thirdly, the condition that the decision must produce 'legal effects' concerning the person at issue or affect him or her 'similarly significantly', it is apparent from the very wording of the first question referred that the action of the third party to whom the probability value is transmitted draws 'strongly' on that value. Thus, according to the factual findings of the referring court, in the event where a loan application is sent by a consumer to a bank, an insufficient probability value leads, in almost all cases, to the refusal of that bank to grant the loan applied for.

It follows that, in circumstances such as those at issue in the main proceedings, in which the probability value established by a credit information agency and communicated to a bank plays a determining role in the granting of credit, the establishment of that value must be qualified in itself as a decision producing vis-à-vis a data subject 'legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly [affecting] him or her' within the meaning of Article 22(1) of the GDPR.

Furthermore, in the case of automated decision-making, such as that referred to in Article 22(1) of the GDPR, first, the controller is subject to additional information obligations under Article 13(2)(f) and Article 14(2)(g) of that regulation. Secondly, the data subject enjoys, under Article 15(1)(h) of that regulation, the right to obtain from the controller, in particular, 'meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject'.

Furthermore, as the Advocate General noted in point 48 of his Opinion, first, the data subject would not be able to assert, from the credit information agency which establishes the probability value concerning him or her, his or her right of access to the specific information referred to in Article 15(1)(h) of the GDPR, in the absence of automated decision-making by that company. Secondly, even assuming that the act adopted by the third party falls within the scope of Article 22(1) of that regulation in so far as it fulfils the conditions for application of that provision, that third party would not be able to provide that specific information because it generally does not have it.

The fact that the establishment of a probability value such as that at issue in the main proceedings is covered by Article 22(1) of the GDPR has the consequence, as noted in paragraphs 53 to 55 of this judgment, that it is prohibited unless one of the exceptions set out in Article 22(2) of that regulation is applicable and the specific requirements provided for in Article 22(3) and (4) of that regulation are complied with.

Thus, in the event that the law of a Member State authorises, under Article 22(2)(b) of the GDPR, the adoption of a decision solely based on automated processing, that processing must comply not only with the conditions set out in the latter provision and in Article 22(4) of that regulation, but also with the requirements set out in Articles 5 and 6 of that regulation. Accordingly, Member States cannot adopt, under Article 22(2)(b) of the GDPR, regulations which authorise profiling in disregard of the requirements laid down by those Articles 5 and 6, as interpreted by the case-law of the Court.

Article 22(1) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value based on personal data relating to a person and concerning his or her ability to meet payment commitments in the future constitutes 'automated individual decision-making' within the meaning of that provision, where a third party, to which that probability value is transmitted, draws strongly on that probability value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.

Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 ... must be interpreted as meaning that the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value based on personal data relating to a person and concerning his or her ability to meet payment commitments in the future constitutes 'automated individual decision-making' within the meaning of that provision, where a third party, to which that probability value is transmitted, draws strongly on that probability value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.

outbound_relations.reasoning: The Court expressly interprets Article 22(1) GDPR as covering the automated establishment of a probability value (scoring) by a credit information agency where a third party draws strongly on that value. This is the principal holding of the judgment and constrains the meaning of the 'decision' element in Article 22(1).
outbound_relations.holding: Article 22(1) GDPR covers the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value concerning a person's ability to meet payment commitments in the future, where a third party draws strongly on that value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.

outbound_relations.reasoning: The holding directs national courts to assess whether Member-State law (e.g. Paragraph 31 BDSG) can serve as a legal basis under Article 22(2)(b) GDPR for automated scoring; the judgment sets out the conditions of lawful authorisation under Article 22(2)(b) and explains how Article 22(2) interacts with Articles 5 and 6 GDPR (paragraphs 65-69).
outbound_relations.holding: Article 22(2)(b) GDPR requires the Member-State law authorising automated individual decision-making to lay down suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and legitimate interests; that law must comply with Articles 5 and 6 GDPR, and Member States are not empowered to add substantive lawfulness rules beyond Article 6(1)(c) and (e).

outbound_relations.reasoning: The Court explicitly affirms (paragraph 66) that the suitable measures required under Article 22(2)(b) and, a fortiori, the safeguards under Article 22(3) include 'at least the right for the data subject to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express his or her point of view and to challenge the decision'; this is a direct interpretation of the safeguards enumerated in Article 22(3).
outbound_relations.holding: Article 22(3) GDPR safeguards (human intervention, expression of point of view, contestation) are integral to any automated decision-making falling within Article 22(1), including scoring by a credit information agency.

outbound_relations.reasoning: The Court holds (paragraph 56, restated in paragraph 63) that the data subject enjoys the right under Article 15(1)(h) GDPR to obtain from the controller that establishes the probability value 'meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing'; without this, the right of access would be hollowed out, as the third-party recipient does not have that information. This is a binding interpretation of Article 15(1)(h), which is part of Article 15(1).
outbound_relations.holding: Article 15(1)(h) GDPR requires the controller that establishes the creditworthiness probability value to disclose meaningful information about the logic involved, the significance and the envisaged consequences of the automated decision-making, lest the data subject's right of access become ineffective in a multi-stakeholder scoring scenario.

judgments.decision_name: VB v Natsionalna agentsia za prihodite (National Revenue Agency, Bulgaria)

citation.full: Judgment of the Court (Third Chamber) of 14 December 2023, VB v Natsionalna agentsia za prihodite, C-340/21, ECLI:EU:C:2023:986
citation.pinpoint: operative part points 1–6 and reasoning paragraphs 39, 47, 52, 57, 64, 74, 80, 81, 82, 84, 85 and 86

judgments.authority: binding preliminary ruling under Article 267 TFEU
judgments.procedural_posture: Reference for a preliminary ruling from the Varhoven administrativen sad (Supreme Administrative Court, Bulgaria) in proceedings brought by an individual affected by the 2019 cyberattack on the Bulgarian National Revenue Agency, seeking non-material damage compensation under Article 82 GDPR.
bounded_holding: Articles 24 and 32 GDPR: unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data by a third party is not sufficient, in itself, to presume that the technical and organisational measures implemented by the controller were not appropriate (paragraphs 31–39, operative point 1).

Article 32 GDPR: the appropriateness of the technical and organisational measures must be assessed by the national courts in a concrete manner, taking into account the risks of the processing and the nature, content and implementation of the measures (paragraphs 42–47, operative point 2).

Article 5(2) read with Article 24 GDPR: in an Article 82 action, the controller bears the burden of proving that the security measures implemented by it are appropriate under Article 32 (paragraphs 49–57, operative point 3).

Article 32 GDPR and the principle of effectiveness: an expert's report cannot constitute a systematically necessary and sufficient means of proof of the appropriateness of the security measures (paragraphs 58–64, operative point 4).

Article 82(3) GDPR: the controller cannot be exempt from compensation under Article 82(1) and (2) solely because the damage is the result of unauthorised access by a third party; the controller must then prove that it is in no way responsible for the event giving rise to the damage (paragraphs 65–74, operative point 5).

Article 82(1) GDPR: the fear experienced by a data subject that his or her personal data might be misused in the future as a result of an infringement of the GDPR is capable, in itself, of constituting 'non-material damage' within the meaning of that provision (paragraphs 75–86, operative point 6).
judgments.later_history: No review or appeal affects this judgment. Builds on and applies the holdings of Case C-300/21 (UI v Österreichische Post) as confirmed authority for the three cumulative conditions and the no-threshold rule (paragraphs 77–78).

judicial_canonical_edges.reasoning: Operative item 1 directly construes Article 2(1) and (2) GDPR to apply to commercial third-country transfers irrespective of subsequent public-authority processing for national-security purposes.
judicial_canonical_edges.holding: Article 2(1) GDPR — the material-scope rule applies to transfers of personal data for commercial purposes by an economic operator established in a Member State to another economic operator established in a third country.

verification_quotes.quote: Therefore, the answer to the first question is that Article 2(1) and (2) of the GDPR must be interpreted as meaning that that regulation applies to the transfer of personal data for commercial purposes by an economic operator established in a Member State to another economic operator established in a third country, irrespective of whether, at the time of that transfer or thereafter, that data is liable to be processed by the authorities of the third country in question for the purposes of public security, defence and State security.

Article 2(1) and (2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 … must be interpreted as meaning that that regulation applies to the transfer of personal data for commercial purposes by an economic operator established in a Member State to another economic operator established in a third country, irrespective of whether, at the time of that transfer or thereafter, that data is liable to be processed by the authorities of the third country in question for the purposes of public security, defence and State security.

judicial_canonical_edges.reasoning: The court considers Article 2(2) (paragraph 84: 'exceptions to the scope of that regulation … must be interpreted strictly') and concludes (paragraph 89) that none of the Article 2(2) exclusions catches the commercial transfer.
judicial_canonical_edges.holding: Article 2(2) GDPR — the listed exclusions do not displace the regulation's application to commercial third-country transfers.

verification_quotes.quote: As to whether such an operation may be regarded as being excluded from the scope of the GDPR under Article 2(2) thereof, it should be noted that that provision lays down exceptions to the scope of that regulation, as defined in Article 2(1) thereof, which must be interpreted strictly (see, by analogy, judgments of 1 December 2011, N.S. and Others, C-411/10 and C-493/10, EU:C:2011:785, paragraphs 77 and 78, and of 8 December 2011, Ziolkowski and Ziolkowska, C-424/10 to C-425/10, EU:C:2011:815, paragraph 32).

judicial_canonical_edges.reasoning: Operative item 5 is a direct validity ruling. The Privacy Shield was adopted under Article 45(3) GDPR but its substantive purpose was to provide a transfer pathway; the court invalidates it because the Commission's finding that the US ensures an adequate level of protection disregarded the requirements of Article 45(3) GDPR read with Articles 7, 8 and 47 of the Charter. Article 45(3) does not have a dedicated 'interprets' edge here because the court did not construe Article 45(3) beyond holding the implementing act invalid; the validity outcome 'invalid' is recorded on this edge. Article 46(1) is the narrowest existing single-paragraph target that the invalidity finding is grounded in (in conjunction with the Charter and the Article 45(3) procedural standard).
judicial_canonical_edges.holding: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 (EU-US Privacy Shield) is invalid.

verification_quotes.quote: Therefore, the ombudsperson mechanism to which the Privacy Shield Decision refers does not provide any cause of action before a body which offers the persons whose data is transferred to the United States guarantees essentially equivalent to those required by Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights.

Therefore, in finding, in Article 1(1) of the Privacy Shield Decision, that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred from the Union to organisations in that third country under the EU-US Privacy Shield, the Commission disregarded the requirements of Article 45(3) of the GDPR, read in the light of Articles 7, 8 and 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights.

Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 of 12 July 2016 pursuant to Directive 95/46/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council on the adequacy of the protection provided by the EU-US Privacy Shield is invalid.

This is the principal holding of the judgment and constrains the meaning of the 'decision' element in Article 22(1).
judicial_canonical_edges.holding: Article 22(1) GDPR covers the automated establishment, by a credit information agency, of a probability value concerning a person's ability to meet payment commitments in the future, where a third party draws strongly on that value to establish, implement or terminate a contractual relationship with that person.

judicial_canonical_edges.reasoning: The holding directs national courts to assess whether Member-State law (e.g. Paragraph 31 BDSG) can serve as a legal basis under Article 22(2)(b) GDPR for automated scoring; the judgment sets out the conditions of lawful authorisation under Article 22(2)(b) and explains how Article 22(2) interacts with Articles 5 and 6 GDPR (paragraphs 65-69).
judicial_canonical_edges.holding: Article 22(2)(b) GDPR requires the Member-State law authorising automated individual decision-making to lay down suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights and legitimate interests; that law must comply with Articles 5 and 6 GDPR, and Member States are not empowered to add substantive lawfulness rules beyond Article 6(1)(c) and (e).

verification_quotes.quote: Thus, in the event that the law of a Member State authorises, under Article 22(2)(b) of the GDPR, the adoption of a decision solely based on automated processing, that processing must comply not only with the conditions set out in the latter provision and in Article 22(4) of that regulation, but also with the requirements set out in Articles 5 and 6 of that regulation.

judicial_canonical_edges.reasoning: The Court explicitly affirms (paragraph 66) that the suitable measures required under Article 22(2)(b) and, a fortiori, the safeguards under Article 22(3) include 'at least the right for the data subject to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express his or her point of view and to challenge the decision'; this is a direct interpretation of the safeguards enumerated in Article 22(3).
judicial_canonical_edges.holding: Article 22(3) GDPR safeguards (human intervention, expression of point of view, contestation) are integral to any automated decision-making falling within Article 22(1), including scoring by a credit information agency.
